course_details.Overview of class: This course will explore the history and nature of photographic imagery relating to its capacity for misrepresentation, with emphasis on context and photography as a contemporary art practice. From the work of 19th century photographers to conceptual artists of the 1980s; from optical lens distortion to post-production manipulation and recent AI applications, we will investigate the age-old issue of truth and its relationship to photography. In addition to more extensive essays, students will write short responses to readings, and produce imagery related to discussion topics.

course_details.Overview of class: This course addresses various problems in painting and introduces students to modes of visual thinking. Work will be done in a two-dimensional format using paint on a gesso-prepared ground on a canvas support. The focus is on acquiring the basic material and technical skills necessary to articulate visual ideas in paint, including how to organize compositions using color and value relationships, form and shape, placement and paint application. Although most exercises deal with problems in painting, considerable work in drawing may be required to support studies in the use of color and paint. Assignments may introduce students to a variety of subject matter, such as still life, landscape and the figure in representational and abstract form. Instruction is individualized and students and faculty participate in one-on-one discussions of works in progress. Students also participate in class discussions and critiques to develop the criteria for making their own judgments about works of visual art. Evaluation is based on the degree of growth, attendance, participation and the degree of mastery of painting materials and techniques.

course_details.Topic: On Violence and the Prefigurative: Abolition, Depo
course_details.Overview of class:
On Violence and the Prefigurative: Abolition, Deposition, Mourning, and Strike

When we grieve communally, we go on a general strike. We demand a suspension and an interruption, the condition of possibility for a beginning that will unfold otherwise. We join forces with the prefigurative, the unthought, and the uncaptured; when we pause, we coalesce with the temporal plasticity of the possible, with that which resists and survives what philosopher María Zambrano calls "sacrificial history."

In this course we will read and respond, through collective and experimental writing, to a series of texts that insists that to change the world means both to invent a new language and to unearth the language of the buried, the unseen, and the unheard. We will focus on the force of the prefigurative and will study forms of counter-history that acknowledge that both the polysemy and ubiquity of violence pose a problem that can only be disentangled through an insurgent poetic transmutation.

Among others prefigurative propositions, we might encounter Rosa Luxemburg's general strike; W.E.B. Du Bois abolition-democracy; Walter Benjamin deposition of the law as a form of counter-violence; Eleni Stecoupoulos's abaton; Denise Ferreira Da Silva's multiple uses of Leibniz's corpus infinitum; Werner Hamacher's afformative strike; Fred Moten's chromatic saturation; Sarah Jaffe's excessive and revolutionary grief; Peter Dimock's injunction to write a love song for imperial times; Paul B. Preciado's dysphoria mundi; Cristina Rivera Garza's forensics of the unbearable in Liliana's Invincible Summer; or Christina Sharpe's wake work. Additionally, all participants will bring their own examples taken from a variety of artistic practices.

course_details.Overview of class:
This studio course explores fiber and textiles as a medium for art making. Students will weave, salvage, deconstruct, piece, embellish, and reimagine materials as art objects, drawing inspiration from contemporary artists who use fiber in their work.
The quarter begins with building frame looms and learning basic weaving techniques to understand how fabric is constructed. The looms will serve as spaces for investigating composition, color, texture, and tension. Alongside weaving, hand-stitching and machine-sewing methods will be introduced as ways to assemble and adorn, with an emphasis on using found fabrics. The final part of the quarter will focus on the sculptural potential of textiles. In addition, a shibori dyeing workshop will give students the opportunity to hand-dye fabric.

Throughout the course, students will be encouraged to think through making and to consider the capacity for metaphor and subversion inherent in fiber-based practices. Assigned readings will examine themes such as craft, labor, and identity. All are welcome to bring their own fiber-based skills and traditions to class, but no prior experience is necessary.

Undergraduate Only.

course_details.Overview of class:
Whether it's an onslaught of images, signs, digital manipulation, or surfaces - the ethos of Collage permeates our contemporary experience. This studio course will examine the historic precedents for contemporary works that blend, sample, layer, cut and paste in both traditional and digital ways. Through research, readings and experimentation, students will create objects that blur the line between Painting, Drawing, Sculpture and Photography.

This course will attempt to decode the current strategies of object making and expand on a field that is continually forcing collisions between increasingly disparate materials and styles.

Undergraduate Only.
